title: Self-Balancing Trees: AVL and Red-Black
summary: Why BSTs need rebalancing, and the rotation/invariant mechanics of AVL and red-black trees — the fix for the degenerate-shape problem from the BST topic.

slides.markdown:
The `binary-search-trees` topic left a specific gap open: a plain BST's height depends entirely on insertion order, and sorted (or adversarial) input degrades it to O(n), turning every operation linear. Self-balancing trees close that gap by enforcing a **height invariant** on every insert and delete, guaranteeing O(log n) height regardless of what order values arrive in.

This topic covers the two classic answers — AVL trees (strict height balance, more rotations, faster lookups) and red-black trees (looser balance, fewer rotations, faster writes) — and, just as importantly, where each actually shows up in production code you'd recognize.

slides.subTitle: The height-difference invariant it enforces
slides.markdown:
An AVL tree maintains one invariant at **every** node: the **balance factor** — height of left subtree minus height of right subtree — must always be -1, 0, or +1. The moment an insert or delete pushes any node's balance factor to -2 or +2, the tree is no longer valid AVL, and a **rotation** (covered next) restores it before the operation is considered complete.

This is a strict guarantee — checked and enforced at *every* node after every mutation, not just occasionally — which is exactly why AVL trees have the tightest height bound of any common self-balancing structure (roughly 1.44 log n in the worst case), at the cost of doing rotation work more often than a looser scheme would need.

slides.subTitle: LL, RR, LR, RL
slides.markdown: ![Four before-and-after mini trees showing the LL, RR, LR, and RL imbalance shapes and their rotation fixes](assets/avl-rotation-cases.svg)

assets.alt: Four before-and-after mini trees showing the LL, RR, LR, and RL imbalance shapes and their rotation fixes

slides.markdown:
```python
def rotate_right(y):
    x = y.left
    y.left = x.right
    x.right = y
    update_height(y)  # y is now lower — recompute its height first
    update_height(x)  # then x, which depends on y's new height
    return x  # new subtree root

def rotate_left(x):
    y = x.right
    x.right = y.left
    y.left = x
    update_height(x)
    update_height(y)
    return y
```

A single rotation (LL or RR) fixes an imbalance that leans straight in one direction. A double rotation (LR or RL) is just two single rotations composed — first rotate the child to convert the zigzag shape into a straight one, then rotate the node itself, exactly the way you'd straighten a bent line by fixing the bend before straightening the whole thing.

slides.subTitle: Leaving stale balance factors
slides.markdown:
```python
# BUG: updates x's height before y's, using y's stale (pre-rotation) height
def rotate_right_wrong(y):
    x = y.left
    y.left = x.right
    x.right = y
    update_height(x)  # WRONG ORDER: x's height depends on y's NEW height,
    update_height(y)  # but y hasn't been recomputed yet
    return x
```

After a rotation, the node that's now **lower** in the tree (`y` in a right rotation) must have its height recomputed **first**, because the node that's now higher (`x`) depends on `y`'s new, post-rotation height to compute its own. Updating in the wrong order uses a stale height value, silently corrupting every balance-factor check computed from that point onward — a bug that often doesn't crash anything, just slowly lets the tree drift out of true balance while every individual check still appears to pass locally.

slides.subTitle: No two red nodes in a row, equal black-height on every path
slides.markdown:
A red-black tree colors every node red or black and enforces a looser set of rules than AVL's strict balance factor: the root is black; no red node has a red child ("no two reds in a row"); and every root-to-null path passes through the **same number** of black nodes (the tree's black-height).

These rules together bound the height at roughly 2 log n in the worst case — looser than AVL's ~1.44 log n, but still logarithmic — while needing fewer rotations to maintain per insert/delete, since a red-black tree tolerates more "slack" imbalance before a rotation is actually required (a color-flip alone often suffices where AVL would need a rotation).

slides.subTitle: Stricter balance and faster lookups vs fewer rotations and faster writes
slides.markdown:
| | AVL | Red-black |
|---|---|---|
| Height bound | ~1.44 log n (tighter) | ~2 log n (looser) |
| Rotations per insert/delete | can require more | typically fewer (color flips often suffice) |
| Lookup speed | faster (shorter paths) | slightly slower (taller paths) |
| Insert/delete speed | slower (more rebalancing) | faster (less rebalancing) |

The trade-off is genuinely about **read-heavy vs write-heavy** workloads: AVL's tighter balance pays off when lookups vastly outnumber mutations, since every lookup benefits from the shorter tree. Red-black's looser balance pays off when inserts and deletes are frequent, since it does less rebalancing work per mutation at the cost of slightly taller trees.

slides.subTitle: TreeMap/std::map as red-black trees under the hood
slides.markdown:
Red-black trees are the far more common choice in production libraries: Java's `TreeMap`/`TreeSet`, C++'s `std::map`/`std::set`, and the Linux kernel's process scheduler all use red-black trees internally. AVL trees are comparatively rare in general-purpose libraries, despite being the one taught first in most courses.

The practical reason tracks the trade-off from the previous slide: most real workloads mix reads and writes rather than being overwhelmingly read-only, and red-black's cheaper rebalancing wins out in that mixed setting. AVL trees do show up in specific niches where lookups genuinely dominate and are performance-critical — some database index implementations, for instance — but as a default general-purpose ordered-map implementation, red-black has won almost everywhere.

slides.subTitle: Most production trees favor red-black's looser balance
slides.markdown:
A common assumption worth correcting: hearing "this uses a balanced tree" and assuming it means AVL's strict ±1 balance factor. In practice, the overwhelming majority of production "balanced trees" you'll encounter are red-black trees, which are balanced in the sense of guaranteeing O(log n) height — but with meaningfully looser tolerance than AVL's definition of balanced.

This matters if you're asked to reason about a specific library's tree performance characteristics: assuming AVL-tight balance for a `std::map` or `TreeMap` will give you a height estimate that's noticeably more optimistic than reality, since red-black's ~2 log n bound is genuinely looser than AVL's ~1.44 log n. "Balanced" is a family of guarantees, not one specific numeric bound — always check which variant a system actually uses before reasoning precisely about its height.

slides.subTitle: Why insert/delete stay O(log n) despite rebalancing
slides.markdown:
A natural worry: if every insert or delete can trigger rebalancing (rotations, recoloring), doesn't that make mutations more expensive than a plain BST's O(h) insert? The answer is no, asymptotically — rebalancing work per operation is itself bounded by O(log n) (at most a constant number of rotations, plus O(log n) recoloring/height-update work walking back up to the root), so the total insert/delete cost stays O(log n), just with a larger constant factor than a plain BST's unbalanced insert.

What you're actually paying for is **worst-case** protection: a plain BST's O(h) insert is only O(log n) if the tree happens to stay balanced by luck of insertion order, with no guarantee; a self-balancing tree pays a slightly higher constant on every single operation in exchange for guaranteeing O(log n) **always**, regardless of insertion order — precisely the guarantee that closes the gap the previous topic's pathological sorted-insertion example exposed.
